title: About this file
short: How many posts, accounts and dates the file has
what_it_shows: A summary of your file: how many posts, how many accounts, the first and last date, the platforms, and which information each post has. It also lists which analyses can run on this file.
how_it_is_calculated: The file is read and cleaned first: empty, deleted or withheld posts are removed and repeated rows are dropped. Then the posts, accounts and dates are counted. Each column is matched to a known type (text, date, account, likes ...).
example: A Meltwater export of 30,000 rows becomes 28,400 posts after removing deleted and empty ones.
good_to_know: If an analysis is greyed out, this card tells you which information is missing from the file.

title: How long are the posts?
short: Words per post, links, hashtags and emoji
what_it_shows: How long the posts are, how many have links, hashtags, mentions or emoji, and how many words are used only once.
how_it_is_calculated: Each post is split into words. Arabic spelling is made uniform first (for example all forms of alef count as one), links and @mentions are left out, and words split on purpose with dots or long dashes are joined again. Then the words in each post are counted.
example: Posts have 18 words on average; 40 % contain a hashtag and 12 % a link.
good_to_know: Very short posts (one or two words) are hard to analyse; this card shows how many there are.

title: Languages and dialects
short: Arabic, English, other languages and Arabic dialects
what_it_shows: Which languages and scripts the posts are written in, how many are written in Arabizi (Arabic in Latin letters), and, with the dialect model, which Arabic dialect region each post comes from.
how_it_is_calculated: Each post's letters are counted: mostly Arabic letters, mostly Latin letters, or a mix. Common small words (the, le, de ...) tell Latin-script languages apart. The dialect step uses a language model trained on 25 Arab cities and Modern Standard Arabic, grouped into regions (Gulf, Levant, Egypt-Sudan, Maghreb, Iraq, Yemen).
example: 78 % of posts are in Arabic, 22 % in English; 5 % are Arabizi such as 'ana mesh 3aref'.
good_to_know: Very short posts are marked 'undetermined'. The dialect model needs a GPU and runs on the MARSAD server or in Colab.

title: Copied and repeated posts
short: How much of the file is the same text posted again
what_it_shows: How many posts are exact copies or almost the same as another post, and which texts are repeated most.
how_it_is_calculated: Each post is cut into short overlapping pieces of three words. Two posts that share most of their pieces (at least 80 %) are counted as near copies. A fast method (MinHash) finds the pairs without comparing every post with every other.
example: The same text posted by 40 accounts counts as one group of 40 copies.
good_to_know: Many copies can mean a campaign, spam or simply retweets. Other analyses can count each repeated text once.

title: Are the posts on topic?
short: Share of posts that really match your search words
what_it_shows: How many posts actually contain the keywords you used to collect the data, so you know how much off-topic material is in the file.
how_it_is_calculated: Each post is checked for each search word as a whole word (not inside another word). If you add a sample that people marked as relevant or not, the card also gives the share of relevant posts with a margin of error.
example: You searched for غزة and Gaza; 85 % of posts contain one of them.
good_to_know: A post can be on topic without the exact keyword, so the keyword share is a lower estimate.

title: Compare files
short: How two or more files differ
what_it_shows: Puts two or more files side by side: size, accounts, dates, attention, kinds of language, and how many accounts and hashtags they share.
how_it_is_calculated: Each file is summarised the same way. Overlap is the number of accounts (or hashtags) found in both files divided by the number found in either file (0 = nothing in common, 1 = the same).
example: File A and file B share 30 % of their accounts and 55 % of their hashtags.
good_to_know: Load two or more files together to use this.

title: Posts over time
short: How many posts each hour, day, week or month
what_it_shows: A line of how many posts were made in each period, with the total and typical attention they got. Click a point to read those posts.
how_it_is_calculated: Each post's date is converted to the time zone you chose. Posts are counted per period; the period (hour, day, week or month) is chosen from how long your data covers. 'Typical attention' is the median: half the posts got more, half got less.
example: Posts jump from 200 a day to 3,000 on the day of an election.
good_to_know: Collection limits (for example a daily download cap) can create dips that are not real.

title: Busiest hours and days
short: At what times people post most
what_it_shows: A grid of days and hours showing when most posts appear, and whether posts at some times get more attention. Weekdays and weekends are compared.
how_it_is_calculated: Each post is placed in its weekday and hour (in your time zone). The cells count posts. The weekend follows the setting (Friday-Saturday or Saturday-Sunday); with 'auto' it is chosen from the countries in the data.
example: Most posts appear at 9 pm on Thursdays.
good_to_know: Times are only as good as the timestamps in the file; posts with no time zone are assumed to be UTC unless you say otherwise.

title: Sudden jumps in posting
short: Days or hours with far more posts than usual
what_it_shows: Finds the days (or hours) when posting suddenly jumped, which often matches news events.
how_it_is_calculated: For each day, the number of posts is compared with the usual level around it (the median of the week centred on that day). A day counts as a jump when it is much higher than usual: more than three times the normal day-to-day variation above it.
example: A normal day has about 100 posts; a day with 900 posts is marked as a jump.
good_to_know: With very few days of data, there is not enough history to call anything a jump.

title: Before and after an event
short: Did things change after a date you choose?
what_it_shows: Compares the days before and after an event you name (for example an election or an attack): number of posts, attention, or the use of a kind of language.
how_it_is_calculated: You give the event a name and a date. Each day's value is calculated, then the days before and the days after are compared, with a test of whether the difference is bigger than chance.
example: Posts per day: 120 in the week before a ceasefire, 340 in the week after.
good_to_know: Other things also happen around big events, so a change is not proof that the event caused it.

title: Most used words
short: The words, hashtags and mentions used most often
what_it_shows: A ranked list of the most frequent words, with how many posts and accounts use each one. Hashtags and @mentions have their own lists.
how_it_is_calculated: Each post is split into words and Arabic spelling is made uniform. Very common small words (and, the, في, من ...) are removed. Then every word is counted. 'Spread' shows whether a word is used by many accounts or only by a few.
example: 'غزة' is used 1,250 times in 900 posts by 300 accounts.
good_to_know: If the same text was posted many times, it can push its words up the list; the card can count repeated posts once.

title: Word cloud
short: The most used words, the bigger the more often
what_it_shows: A picture of the most used words: the bigger the word, the more often it appears. Click a word to read the posts that use it.
how_it_is_calculated: Words are counted as in 'Most used words'. Each word's size grows with how often it is used. The position of a word in the cloud has no meaning.
example: 'الانتخابات' is drawn largest because it is the most used word.
good_to_know: Use 'Most used words' for exact numbers.

title: Emoji cloud
short: Which emoji people used
what_it_shows: The emoji used in the posts, the bigger the more often, and how many posts contain emoji. Click an emoji for its posts.
how_it_is_calculated: Every emoji in every post is counted. Emoji made of several parts, such as flags, skin tones and families, are kept together as one emoji.
example: The crying face is the most used emoji, in 8 % of posts.
good_to_know: Emoji can be used ironically, so read some posts before drawing conclusions.

title: Words that stand out
short: Words used much more here than in normal language
what_it_shows: The words that are unusually common in your posts (or in one group of posts) compared with everyday language or with the rest of your data. These 'key words' show what is special about the conversation.
how_it_is_calculated: For each word, its share in your posts is compared with its share in a reference: everyday language (word frequencies from Wikipedia, subtitles, news and social media), or another part of your data. A statistical score (log-likelihood) says if the difference is real, and the 'how much more' number (log ratio) says how big it is.
example: 'ceasefire' is 40 times more common in your posts than in everyday English, so it stands out.
good_to_know: Names and very rare words can stand out just because they are rare; the card needs a word to appear in several posts.

title: Find a word in the posts
short: Read every sentence where a word appears
what_it_shows: Type a word or phrase and see every place it appears, with the words just before and after it, lined up so you can compare how it is used.
how_it_is_calculated: The word is searched as a whole word. For Arabic, common attached letters such as و and ال are allowed, so searching غزة also finds وغزة and بغزة. Each line shows a few words on each side.
example: Searching 'الأمل' shows every sentence with it, for example '... ما زال الأمل موجودا ...'.
good_to_know: Use * as a wildcard, for example فلسطين* .

title: Words that go together
short: Which words often appear next to a word
what_it_shows: For a word you choose, the words that often appear close to it. This shows what people connect it with.
how_it_is_calculated: Around each use of your word, the five words on each side are collected. Each nearby word is counted, and a score says if it appears near your word more often than chance would give.
example: Next to 'حرب' the most common partners are 'إبادة', 'غزة' and 'وقف'.
good_to_know: Words that are common everywhere get lower scores, so the list favours real partners.

title: Phrases around a word
short: Common phrases that start or end with a word
what_it_shows: The fixed phrases people build around a word (for example 'the people of ...'), with how often each phrase is used.
how_it_is_calculated: Every sequence of two to four words that starts or ends with your word is counted, with the number of posts and accounts using it.
example: Around 'people' the most common phrase is 'the people of Gaza'.
good_to_know: Choose the phrase length and whether the word comes first or last in the settings.

title: A word over time
short: When a word was used, and by how many accounts
what_it_shows: How often one or more words were used in each period, so you can see when a word became popular.
how_it_is_calculated: For each period, the uses of the word are counted per 1,000 words of all posts in that period (so busy days do not look bigger just because there are more posts). A strip shows one mark for each post that uses the word.
example: 'ceasefire' goes from 2 to 15 uses per 1,000 words in the week of the talks.
good_to_know: Type several words separated by commas to compare them.

title: How rich is the vocabulary?
short: Do some groups use more varied words?
what_it_shows: Compares groups (for example accounts, countries or files) on how varied their words are, how long their posts are and how many of their words are Arabic.
how_it_is_calculated: Vocabulary variety is the number of different words in each window of 50 words, averaged over all posts. This makes groups with long and short texts comparable. A range shows how certain the result is.
example: News pages use 40 different words per 50 words; personal accounts use 32.
good_to_know: Small groups give unstable numbers; compare groups with many posts.

title: Main topics
short: Groups of posts that talk about the same thing
what_it_shows: Puts posts that talk about the same thing into groups (topics) and names each group by its most typical words. Shows the biggest topics, how they change over time and a map where similar posts sit close together.
how_it_is_calculated: Each post is turned into a list of numbers that describes its meaning (a 'sentence embedding'). Posts with similar meaning get similar numbers. A grouping method (HDBSCAN) then finds dense groups of similar posts; posts that fit no group are called outliers. A quality score from -1 to 1 (silhouette) says how well separated the groups are: above 0.5 is good.
example: 320 posts about prices and wages form one topic, named 'prices, wages, rising, cost'.
good_to_know: Topic names are made from words, so read the example posts before you name a topic yourself. Each run is saved so you can compare settings.

title: Words used in the same way
short: A map of words that appear in similar sentences
what_it_shows: A map where words that are used in similar sentences sit close together, and groups of such words.
how_it_is_calculated: A small language model (FastText) learns from your own posts which words appear in similar surroundings. Words with similar surroundings get similar positions on the map.
example: 'هدنة', 'وقف' and 'تهدئة' sit close together because they are used in the same sentences.
good_to_know: Needs at least 200 posts, and runs in Colab or on the MARSAD server.

title: Posts about an idea
short: Find posts close in meaning to an idea you describe
what_it_shows: You describe an idea in a sentence (in any language). The card finds the posts closest to that idea in meaning, even when they use other words.
how_it_is_calculated: Your sentence and every post are turned into meaning numbers by a multilingual language model. The closer two lists of numbers are, the closer the meaning (cosine similarity from 0 to 1).
example: You describe 'people asking for medical help'; the card finds posts about hospitals and medicine.
good_to_know: Needs a language model, so it runs in Colab or on the MARSAD server.

title: Positive or negative?
short: Is each post positive, negative or neutral?
what_it_shows: How many posts are positive, negative or neutral, how this changes over time, and which kind gets more attention. Click a part of a chart to read those posts.
how_it_is_calculated: A language model reads each post and gives it one of three labels with a confidence score. The default model (multilingual DistilBERT) understands 12 languages, including Arabic, English and French. Posts in other languages are left out and counted.
example: 'What a great day for our team' is positive; 'Prices are rising again' is negative.
good_to_know: Models make mistakes, especially with sarcasm and dialect. Check a sample by hand before reporting numbers.

title: Emotions
short: Anger, fear, joy or sadness
what_it_shows: Which emotion each post mostly expresses (anger, fear, joy or sadness), and how emotions change over time.
how_it_is_calculated: A multilingual language model (XLM-EMO), trained on emotion data in 19 languages including Arabic, gives each post the emotion it finds strongest, with a confidence score.
example: 'I am so scared for my family' is labelled fear.
good_to_know: Only four emotions are covered; a post with no clear emotion still gets one of the four.

title: Toxic language
short: How rude, insulting or threatening the language is
what_it_shows: A toxicity score from 0 (not toxic) to 1 (very toxic) for each post, with separate scores for insults, threats, obscene words and attacks on identity, and the posts that score highest.
how_it_is_calculated: For English, French, Spanish, Italian, Portuguese, Turkish and Russian, the Detoxify model gives seven scores. For Arabic and other languages, the TextDetox model gives one overall score. A post counts as toxic when its score is 0.7 or more (you can change this).
example: An insult gets a toxicity score of 0.92; a news headline gets 0.03.
good_to_know: Toxicity models can mark reclaimed words or quotes as toxic. Read the highest-scoring posts.

title: Hate speech
short: Posts attacking people for who they are
what_it_shows: Which posts are hate speech: attacks on people because of their religion, origin, gender or another part of who they are.
how_it_is_calculated: A language model trained on hate speech data (DeHateBERT, one model for Arabic and one for English) labels each post 'hate' or 'not hate' with a confidence score. Posts in other languages are left out and counted.
example: A post calling a whole religious group animals is labelled hate speech.
good_to_know: Hate speech is hard to judge; have people check a sample. MARSAD's own hate speech model can replace this one.

title: For or against?
short: Do posts support or oppose a person, group or idea?
what_it_shows: For a target you name (a person, a party, a policy), whether posts support it, oppose it or are neutral.
how_it_is_calculated: A language model that understands many languages (mDeBERTa, trained on natural language inference) checks each post against sentences like 'This text supports X' and 'This text opposes X' and picks the best fit. It runs on a random sample.
example: For the target 'the new tax', 'This tax will ruin us' is labelled against.
good_to_know: This kind of model is not trained on your topic; check a sample by hand.

title: Political leaning
short: Which political side a post leans to
what_it_shows: The political leaning of each post (for example left, centre or right, or for or against a party), over time and by language.
how_it_is_calculated: MARSAD's political bias model reads each post and gives it a label with a confidence score.
example: A post praising lower taxes and smaller government may be labelled right-leaning.
good_to_know: Coming soon: needs the MARSAD political bias service to be connected.

title: Kinds of language over time
short: How often words of hope, fear, anger and others appear
what_it_shows: The share of posts that use a kind of language (for example hope, fear, victimhood, religious words), and how it changes over time or between groups.
how_it_is_calculated: Each post is checked against expert word lists (for example words of hope, words of fear, 'us' and 'them' words). Words must match as whole words; for Arabic, common attached letters such as و and ال are allowed. The card shows the share of posts with at least one match, and the number of matches per 1,000 words.
example: Hope words appear in 12 % of posts in January and 20 % in March.
good_to_know: Word lists catch words, not meaning: 'no hope' still counts as a hope word. Check the word lists first.

title: Compare two kinds of language
short: Which of two framings wins, and when?
what_it_shows: Compares two kinds of language (for example hope and despair) and shows which one is used more, and how that balance changes over time.
how_it_is_calculated: Each post is checked against expert word lists (for example words of hope, words of fear, 'us' and 'them' words). Words must match as whole words; for Arabic, common attached letters such as و and ال are allowed. For each period, the matches of the first list are divided by the matches of both lists together (above 50 % means the first list wins).
example: Hope words are 60 % and despair words 40 % of all hope and despair matches.
good_to_know: Both lists should be similar in size, or the bigger list will look stronger.

title: Kinds of language used together
short: Which kinds of language appear in the same posts
what_it_shows: Shows how often two or three kinds of language appear in the same post, for example anger together with religion.
how_it_is_calculated: Each post is checked against expert word lists (for example words of hope, words of fear, 'us' and 'them' words). Words must match as whole words; for Arabic, common attached letters such as و and ال are allowed. Posts are grouped by which lists they match. 'Lift' says how much more often two lists appear together than chance would give (1 = chance, 2 = twice as often).
example: Anger and religious words appear together 2.5 times more often than chance.
good_to_know: Rare lists give unstable numbers.

title: We, you and they
short: Who the posts talk about, and how sure they sound
what_it_shows: How often posts say 'we', 'you' or 'they', and whether they use strong words (must, will) or careful words (may, perhaps).
how_it_is_calculated: Each post is checked against expert word lists (for example words of hope, words of fear, 'us' and 'them' words). Words must match as whole words; for Arabic, common attached letters such as و and ال are allowed. Pronouns and certainty words are counted per 1,000 words.
example: 'We' appears 8 times per 1,000 words, 'they' 12 times.
good_to_know: Arabic often hides pronouns inside the verb, so counts are a lower estimate.

title: How groups talk differently
short: Compare the language of accounts, countries or files
what_it_shows: For each group (for example each country or each file), how much it uses each kind of language, and which groups talk most alike.
how_it_is_calculated: Each post is checked against expert word lists (for example words of hope, words of fear, 'us' and 'them' words). Words must match as whole words; for Arabic, common attached letters such as و and ال are allowed. Matches are counted per 1,000 words for each group. Groups are compared by how similar their whole profile is (1 = identical mix of language).
example: Accounts from Qatar use more hope words; accounts from Egypt more economic words.
good_to_know: Groups need enough posts (30 or more by default) to be compared.

title: My own word list
short: Count any words you type
what_it_shows: Type your own words (for example names of places or slogans) and see how often they appear, over time or by group.
how_it_is_calculated: Each post is checked against expert word lists (for example words of hope, words of fear, 'us' and 'them' words). Words must match as whole words; for Arabic, common attached letters such as و and ال are allowed. Your words are checked the same way as the expert lists.
example: You type 'حماس, Hamas'; the card shows they appear in 9 % of posts.
good_to_know: Add spelling variants yourself if needed.

title: Most active accounts
short: Who posted most, and who got most attention
what_it_shows: A ranked list of accounts by number of posts and by attention received (likes, comments, shares), with their first and last post.
how_it_is_calculated: Posts and attention are added up for each account. 'Share' is the account's part of all posts or all attention.
example: The most active page posted 340 times, 4 % of all posts.
good_to_know: Large pages naturally get more attention; see 'What gets more attention?' for fair comparisons.

title: Few voices or many?
short: Is the conversation led by a few accounts?
what_it_shows: Whether a few accounts make most of the posts (or get most of the attention), or whether many accounts share the conversation.
how_it_is_calculated: The share of posts made by the 10 most active accounts and by the top 1 % of accounts is calculated. The Gini score sums this up from 0 (everyone posts the same amount) to 1 (one account posts everything). A curve shows the whole picture.
example: The 10 most active accounts made 46 % of all posts: a few voices lead.
good_to_know: Collections built from a list of pages are concentrated by design.

title: Who posts regularly?
short: Steady posters and bursts
what_it_shows: How regularly each account posts (every day or in bursts) and whether posting more on a day brings more or less attention per post.
how_it_is_calculated: For each account: number of days with posts, posts per active day, and how much its daily attention goes up and down.
example: One page posts every day; another posts 50 times on one day and then stops.
good_to_know: Needs account names and dates.

title: Who talks to whom?
short: A map of replies, mentions, shared links or hashtags
what_it_shows: A network map: circles are accounts (or hashtags or websites), lines show who replies to, mentions or quotes whom. Colours show communities: groups of accounts that interact more with each other. Click a circle to read what it sent and received.
how_it_is_calculated: Every reply, mention, quote or shared link becomes a line between two circles; more posts make a stronger line. A community method (Louvain) finds groups with many lines inside and few lines between them. A circle's size shows how many replies or mentions it receives. You can search, filter by dates or keep only toxic connections.
example: Accounts A and B reply to each other often, so they sit close together in the same colour group.
good_to_know: Some exports do not include replies (for example Meltwater for X), so the map shows only what is in the file.

title: Unusual accounts
short: Accounts that post very often, very regularly or repeat themselves
what_it_shows: Accounts with unusual behaviour: many posts in one day, posting at very regular intervals, or repeating the same text.
how_it_is_calculated: For each account: most posts in one day, the time between its posts and how regular it is, how spread over the day its posting is, and how much of its text is repeated.
example: An account that posts every 60 seconds, all day, is flagged as unusual.
good_to_know: This is a reason to look closer, not proof of a bot.

title: Countries
short: Where posts come from
what_it_shows: Posts, accounts and attention per country.
how_it_is_calculated: Posts are counted per country as given in the file. The card says whether the country is the page's or the author's.
example: 45 % of posts come from pages in Egypt, 20 % from Saudi Arabia.
good_to_know: Many exports give the page administrator's country, not where the writer lives.

title: Types of pages
short: News pages, politicians, communities ... (CrowdTangle)
what_it_shows: Which kinds of Facebook pages (media, public figures, community groups ...) lead the conversation and which get more attention.
how_it_is_calculated: Facebook's detailed page categories are grouped into main types, then compared on posts and attention.
example: News pages make 30 % of posts but get 55 % of shares.
good_to_know: Only CrowdTangle files have page categories.

title: Older pages vs newer pages
short: Do older pages get more attention? (CrowdTangle)
what_it_shows: Whether pages that have existed longer get more attention than new pages.
how_it_is_calculated: Each page's age when it posted is compared with its typical attention, using a rank correlation from -1 to 1 (0 = no link).
example: Pages older than 10 years get no more attention than new pages (score close to 0).
good_to_know: Only CrowdTangle files have the page creation date.

title: Likes, comments and shares
short: How much attention posts got
what_it_shows: How likes, comments and shares are spread over posts: typical values, the most successful posts and how much of all attention goes to the top 1 % and 10 % of posts.
how_it_is_calculated: All attention numbers are put in order. The median is the middle post; percentiles show the values that 90 % or 99 % of posts stay below. A few posts with huge numbers are flagged as outliers.
example: Half the posts get fewer than 25 interactions; the top 1 % of posts get 40 % of all interactions.
good_to_know: Attention is usually very uneven: a few posts get most of it.

title: What gets more attention?
short: Posts with hashtags, links, questions, videos ...
what_it_shows: Compares posts with and without a feature (hashtags, links, questions, length, posting hour ...) to see which get more attention.
how_it_is_calculated: Posts are put in groups by the feature. To be fair to small and large pages, each post is also compared with its own account's usual attention. A test says if the difference is bigger than chance.
example: Posts with a video get twice the typical attention of posts with only text.
good_to_know: A feature that goes with more attention does not always cause it.

title: Do certain words get more attention?
short: Attention for posts with a kind of language
what_it_shows: Whether posts that use a kind of language (for example anger words) get more or less attention than other posts.
how_it_is_calculated: Posts are split into those with and without matches from the word list, then compared as in 'What gets more attention?'.
example: Posts with anger words get 30 % more shares than other posts.
good_to_know: Check the word list first; see 'Kinds of language over time'.

title: Mix of reactions
short: Shares compared with likes and comments
what_it_shows: The balance between kinds of attention, for example how many shares a post gets for every like.
how_it_is_calculated: Shares, comments and likes are divided by each other, for all posts together and for the typical post.
example: On average a post gets 1 share for every 8 likes.
good_to_know: A high share-to-like ratio often means people pass the post on rather than just agree.

title: Love, Haha, Angry and other reactions
short: Facebook reactions over time
what_it_shows: The share of each Facebook reaction (Love, Haha, Wow, Sad, Angry, Care) and how it changes over time.
how_it_is_calculated: Reactions are added up, likes are left out, and each reaction's share is calculated per period.
example: Angry is 40 % of all reactions in the week of the attack, 10 % the week before.
good_to_know: Only files with Facebook reactions (CrowdTangle, Meta Content Library).

title: Did the audience react positively?
short: A reaction score from negative to positive
what_it_shows: A score from -1 (very negative audience reaction) to +1 (very positive) for each post, and whether the audience was divided.
how_it_is_calculated: Love counts as positive, Angry and Sad as negative, using this formula: (2 Love - 2 Angry - Sad) divided by all reactions. Only posts with at least 10 reactions are used. 'Divided' means many positive and many negative reactions on the same post.
example: A post with 200 Love and 10 Angry scores close to +1 (positive).
good_to_know: This is the audience's reaction, not the tone of the post itself.

title: Attention compared with audience size
short: Engagement per 100 followers
what_it_shows: How much attention a post gets compared with the number of followers of the page, so small and large pages can be compared.
how_it_is_calculated: Likes, comments and shares are added and divided by the number of followers at posting time, then multiplied by 100.
example: A small page with 1,000 followers and 100 interactions scores 10 per 100 followers.
good_to_know: Needs the follower count in the file.

title: Views
short: How many views, and attention per view
what_it_shows: Views per post, likes and comments per view, and views per follower.
how_it_is_calculated: Views are taken from the file; attention is divided by views.
example: A video with 10,000 views and 500 interactions has 5 interactions per 100 views.
good_to_know: Only files with a views column.

title: Posts that did better than usual
short: Posts above their page's normal level (CrowdTangle)
what_it_shows: Which posts did much better (or worse) than their page usually does.
how_it_is_calculated: Uses CrowdTangle's score, which compares each post with the page's recent posts of the same type.
example: A post with score 3.0 did three times better than the page usually does.
good_to_know: Only CrowdTangle files.

title: Videos
short: Video length, ownership and attention (CrowdTangle)
what_it_shows: Whether longer or shorter videos, own videos or shared videos get more attention.
how_it_is_calculated: Videos are put into length groups and compared on attention; attention per minute of video is also shown.
example: Videos under one minute get more interactions per minute than long videos.
good_to_know: Only CrowdTangle files with video information.

title: Messages copied across accounts
short: Which texts spread, how fast and through how many accounts
what_it_shows: Messages that were posted again and again (the same or almost the same words), with how many accounts posted them, when they first and last appeared, and how fast they spread.
how_it_is_calculated: Near copies are found as in 'Copied and repeated posts'. For each group of copies: posts, accounts, platforms, first and last date, and the number of posts in the first 24 hours.
example: The same slogan was posted by 120 accounts within 6 hours.
good_to_know: To find messages with the same meaning but different words, use 'Claims people made'.

title: Websites people linked to
short: Which news sites and sources were shared
what_it_shows: The websites linked most often, and how many links were hidden behind link shorteners (like bit.ly).
how_it_is_calculated: Links are taken from the text and link columns, and reduced to the website name (www and mobile versions are merged).
example: youtube.com is linked in 300 posts; 15 % of links use bit.ly or similar shorteners.
good_to_know: You can add your own list of trusted or untrusted sites.

title: Accounts posting together
short: Groups that post the same thing at the same moment
what_it_shows: Groups of accounts that posted the same text or link within seconds of each other, more than once. This can be a sign of a coordinated campaign.
how_it_is_calculated: An event is the same text or link posted by at least 3 accounts within 60 seconds. Accounts that share at least 2 events are linked, and linked accounts form a group.
example: Five accounts posted the same link within 20 seconds, on four different days.
good_to_know: Coordination can be harmless (for example a news agency and its partners).

title: Conversations and replies
short: How long and how deep reply threads are
what_it_shows: How many replies posts get, how deep conversations go (replies to replies) and, with labels, how tone changes deeper in a thread.
how_it_is_calculated: Reply trees are built from the 'reply to' information in the file. Depth is the number of steps from the first post.
example: A Reddit post with 80 replies, going 6 replies deep.
good_to_know: Needs reply information (for example Reddit or Communalytic files).

title: How far views travelled
short: Views beyond the original post (CrowdTangle)
what_it_shows: How many more views a post got through copies and shares compared with its own views.
how_it_is_calculated: Total views divided by the original post's views.
example: A video with 10,000 views on the page and 50,000 in total travelled 5 times further.
good_to_know: Only CrowdTangle files with both view counts.

title: Reach and sources (Meltwater)
short: Meltwater reach, sources and sentiment
what_it_shows: Meltwater's own numbers: estimated reach, advertising value, sources, languages and Meltwater's sentiment labels over time.
how_it_is_calculated: The numbers come from Meltwater and are added up or counted.
example: Meltwater reports a reach of 2 million for the week; 60 % from X.
good_to_know: Reach is the possible audience, not the people who actually saw a post.

title: Posts worth fact-checking
short: Posts that make a claim someone should check
what_it_shows: Which posts make a factual claim that is worth checking (and not just an opinion), and how many there are over time.
how_it_is_calculated: MARSAD's check-worthiness model reads each post and says whether it contains a claim worth fact-checking, with a confidence score.
example: 'The minister said unemployment fell to 3 %' is worth checking; 'I hate Mondays' is not.
good_to_know: Coming soon: needs the MARSAD check-worthiness service to be connected.

title: Claims people made
short: The claims in the posts, and which are repeated most
what_it_shows: The factual claims found in the posts, written as short sentences, grouped when they say the same thing, and ranked by how many posts and accounts made them.
how_it_is_calculated: MARSAD's claim extraction service writes out the claims in each post. Claims with almost the same wording are grouped (by comparing letter patterns), and the most common wording is shown.
example: 'Prices doubled in one month' is found in 120 posts with slightly different wording.
good_to_know: Coming soon: needs the MARSAD claim extraction service to be connected.

title: Fact check results
short: Are the claims supported, refuted or unclear?
what_it_shows: For each post or claim: whether the evidence supports it, refutes it or is not enough, with a score and the evidence found.
how_it_is_calculated: MARSAD's fact verification service searches for evidence and compares the claim with it, then gives a verdict and a veracity score.
example: 'Prices doubled in one month' is labelled refuted, with official price data as the evidence.
good_to_know: Coming soon: needs the MARSAD fact verification service. Always read the evidence before calling a post false.

title: Propaganda
short: Posts that use propaganda
what_it_shows: Which posts use propaganda, how many there are over time, and which get more attention.
how_it_is_calculated: MARSAD's propaganda model reads each post and labels it 'propaganda' or 'not propaganda' with a confidence score.
example: A post that calls a group traitors and repeats a slogan may be labelled propaganda.
good_to_know: Coming soon: needs the MARSAD propaganda service to be connected.

title: Propaganda techniques
short: Name calling, exaggeration, slogans, fear and other tricks
what_it_shows: Which propaganda techniques are used (for example name calling, exaggeration, appeals to fear, slogans, flag-waving) and how often.
how_it_is_calculated: MARSAD's technique model finds every technique in each post; one post can use several. Techniques are counted and followed over time.
example: 'These traitors will destroy our nation!' uses name calling and appeal to fear.
good_to_know: Coming soon: needs the MARSAD propaganda technique service to be connected.

title: Download my report
short: Save the charts you collected
what_it_shows: Puts the analyses you added to your report into one file you can keep or share: an interactive web page, PDF, LaTeX, CSV or JSON.
how_it_is_calculated: Each saved analysis is exported with its chart, tables, settings and the 'good to know' notes.
example: Save five charts, then download one web page with all of them.

title: Pick posts to label by hand
short: A fair sample of posts for people to check
what_it_shows: Draws a fair random sample of posts (for example the same number from each month or each group) into a spreadsheet for people to label, and checks how much two people agree.
how_it_is_calculated: Posts are drawn at random within each group you choose. Agreement between two people is measured with Cohen's kappa (1 = full agreement, 0 = no better than chance).
example: Draw 50 posts per month for two people to label as relevant or not.
good_to_know: Use it to check a model or a word list on your own data.

title: Dataset description sheet
short: A ready-made description of your data for a paper
what_it_shows: Writes a standard description of your dataset (a 'datasheet'): where it comes from, what it covers, how it was cleaned and its limits.
how_it_is_calculated: The sheet is filled in from the file and the settings; you add what only you know (purpose, ethics approval, collection method).
example: A one-page description of the dataset for the data section of a paper.

title: Social cohesion
short: How connected and united is the conversation?
what_it_shows: A score from 0 (divided) to 100 (cohesive), built from up to seven parts: are accounts connected, do groups talk to each other, do they share topics, do people say 'we' more than 'them', do they humanize others, is the tone civil, and do audiences react the same way.
how_it_is_calculated: Each part is scored from 0 to 100 using what the file has. Connected: share of accounts in the biggest group linked by replies or mentions. Bridging: share of replies or mentions between different groups. Shared agenda: how many of their top hashtags the most active accounts have in common. Us, not them: 'we' words out of 'we' plus 'them' words. Humanizing: humanizing words out of humanizing plus dehumanizing words. Civil tone: share of posts not toxic. Audience agreement: how much people reacting to a post chose the same reaction. The index is the average of the parts found (or MARSAD's own formula, once added).
example: Bridging 20 means one reply in five goes to another group; Us, not them 70 means 'we' words outnumber 'them' words.
good_to_know: Only compare scores between files that use the same parts. The language parts use word lists that are not yet validated.

title: Emotional intensity
short: How heated is the writing?
what_it_shows: How heated the posts look: exclamation marks, stretched letters, words in capitals, emoji, intensifiers (very, so) and emotion words, over time or by group, and whether intense posts get more attention.
how_it_is_calculated: Each sign is counted in every post. Intensity = number of signs per 10 words. The card also shows the share of posts with each sign and the most intense posts.
example: 'هذا ظلللم!!! 😡😡' has 4 signs of intensity in 2 words: a score of 20 per 10 words.
good_to_know: It measures how the writing looks, not what the writer feels.

title: Distress and resilience
short: Trauma, exhaustion and grief, or steadfastness and hope?
what_it_shows: How often posts use words of trauma and fear, exhaustion, shared grief, and how often they use words of steadfastness and hope, over time or by group.
how_it_is_calculated: Each post is checked against five MARSAD word lists. The card shows the share of posts with at least one match and the number of matches per 1,000 words, for each list.
example: Grief words rise from 3 % to 15 % of posts after a disaster, while resilience words stay at 5 %.
good_to_know: Word lists catch words, not states of mind. It is a signal of public mood, not a diagnosis of anyone.

title: Economic concern
short: Prices, jobs, poverty, inequality and corruption
what_it_shows: How much the conversation is about the economy: prices, unemployment, poverty, inequality and corruption, and when this rises.
how_it_is_calculated: Each post is checked against three MARSAD word lists (economic conditions, economic justice, corruption). The card shows the share of posts with at least one match and the matches per 1,000 words.
example: Words like 'prices', 'rent' and 'غلاء' appear in 18 % of posts in the month prices rose.
good_to_know: Useful next to price or unemployment data for the same period.

title: Calls to action
short: Do posts call people to act or propose solutions?
what_it_shows: How often posts say 'together we can', propose solutions, ask people to share or join, or use protest words.
how_it_is_calculated: Each post is checked against four MARSAD word lists. The card shows the share of posts with at least one match and the matches per 1,000 words, over time or by group.
example: 'Share this and join us on Friday' matches the call to share and protest lists.
good_to_know: A call to share is not the same as a call to protest; look at each list separately.

title: Blame and accountability
short: Who is blamed, and do people ask for accountability?
what_it_shows: How often posts blame someone, speak of injustice, or ask for accountability (trials, sanctions, investigations).
how_it_is_calculated: Each post is checked against three MARSAD word lists. The card shows the share of posts with at least one match and the matches per 1,000 words. Use 'Find a word in the posts' to see who is blamed.
example: 'The government is responsible, we demand an investigation' matches blame and accountability.
good_to_know: The word lists find blame words, not the person blamed.

title: Identity and belonging
short: Nation, 'we' and gender in the conversation
what_it_shows: How often posts talk about the nation and homeland, use 'we' and 'our people', and mention gender.
how_it_is_calculated: Each post is checked against four MARSAD word lists. The card shows the share of posts with at least one match and the matches per 1,000 words.
example: 'Our homeland', 'our people' and 'Qatar' match the national identity and 'we' lists.
good_to_know: Compare groups (for example countries) with the 'Split the results by' option.

title: Trust in institutions
short: Trust or distrust in government, media, courts, health, science
what_it_shows: How often posts express trust (credible, we trust, well done) or distrust (they lied, cover-up, empty promises), and how often they name an institution, over time or by group.
how_it_is_calculated: Each post is checked against MARSAD word lists in Arabic (standard Arabic and common Gulf, Egyptian, Levantine and Maghrebi forms) and English. The card shows, for each list, the share of posts with at least one match and the matches per 1,000 words. The balance is the share of posts on the first side among posts with words from either side (a post with both counts on both sides). 'Not' before a word cancels it (مش مبسوط is not counted as happy). The trust share is also given for posts that name an institution.
example: 'They lied to us again' counts as distrust; 'thank you to the ministry, well done' as trust. Trust share 30 % = 3 trust posts for every 7 distrust posts.
good_to_know: Distrust words are more common than trust words in most public talk, so watch the change over time more than the level. The word lists do not tell which institution is trusted: read the posts.

title: Moral values
short: Care, fairness, loyalty, authority, sanctity
what_it_shows: Which moral values posts appeal to, following Moral Foundations Theory: care or harm, fairness or cheating, loyalty or betrayal, respect for authority or chaos, sanctity or disgust.
how_it_is_calculated: Each post is checked against MARSAD word lists in Arabic (standard Arabic and common Gulf, Egyptian, Levantine and Maghrebi forms) and English. The card shows, for each list, the share of posts with at least one match and the matches per 1,000 words. Each value has two lists, the virtue and the vice. The balance is the share of posts on the first side among posts with words from either side (a post with both counts on both sides). 'Not' before a word cancels it (مش مبسوط is not counted as happy).
example: 'Protect the children' is care; 'نقف معكم يد واحدة' is loyalty; 'غير عادل' is cheating. Fairness share 40 % = more posts about injustice than about justice.
good_to_know: Common words like law, rights and kill are in the lists, so news posts score too. Compare groups or periods of the same kind of posts. Our own lists, not a translation of the English Moral Foundations Dictionary.

title: Wellbeing
short: Positive feelings, engagement, relationships, meaning, accomplishment
what_it_shows: Public signs of wellbeing using the five PERMA parts: positive feelings (happy, grateful), engagement (passion, learning), relationships (friends, family, support), meaning (purpose, volunteering) and accomplishment (success, graduated, proud).
how_it_is_calculated: Each post is checked against MARSAD word lists in Arabic (standard Arabic and common Gulf, Egyptian, Levantine and Maghrebi forms) and English. The card shows, for each list, the share of posts with at least one match and the matches per 1,000 words.
example: During a holiday, 'فرحانين' and 'لمة العيلة' posts rise: positive feelings and relationships go up.
good_to_know: For groups and periods only, never a judgment about one person. Public posts show what people choose to share, not how they feel. Needs ethics review before use in a study.

title: Stress and coping
short: How much stress people express, and how they cope
what_it_shows: How often posts express stress (pressure, can't sleep, fed up, مخنوق, زهقت) and coping (taking a break, talking it out, prayer, adapting), with exhaustion words, over time or by group.
how_it_is_calculated: Each post is checked against MARSAD word lists in Arabic (standard Arabic and common Gulf, Egyptian, Levantine and Maghrebi forms) and English. The card shows, for each list, the share of posts with at least one match and the matches per 1,000 words. The balance is the share of posts on the first side among posts with words from either side (a post with both counts on both sides). 'Not' before a word cancels it (مش مبسوط is not counted as happy). The coping share compares coping with stress and exhaustion.
example: During exam weeks 'ضغط الامتحانات' and 'ما نمت' rise from 2 % to 6 % of student posts; coping share drops from 45 % to 30 %.
good_to_know: A rise in stress words during a crisis is a public signal, not a diagnosis. Religious coping (الدعاء, الاستغفار) is counted as coping.

title: Certainty and self-focus
short: Certain or doubtful? 'I' or 'we'?
what_it_shows: How often posts use words of certainty (definitely, no doubt, اكيد) or doubt (maybe, I think, مدري), and 'I' words or 'we' words, over time or by group.
how_it_is_calculated: Each post is checked against MARSAD word lists in Arabic (standard Arabic and common Gulf, Egyptian, Levantine and Maghrebi forms) and English. The card shows, for each list, the share of posts with at least one match and the matches per 1,000 words. The balance is the share of posts on the first side among posts with words from either side (a post with both counts on both sides). 'Not' before a word cancels it (مش مبسوط is not counted as happy). 'I rather than we' compares posts with 'I' words to posts with 'we' words.
example: 'Definitely, no doubt' is certainty; 'maybe, I think' is doubt. Certainty share 70 % = 7 certain posts for every 3 doubtful ones.
good_to_know: Arabic often marks 'I' inside the verb (قلت) or with an ending (كتابي), which word lists cannot see, so Arabic 'I' counts are low. Compare Arabic with Arabic and English with English.

title: Economic mood
short: Worries and shortages, or good economic news?
what_it_shows: How often posts talk about economic worries (prices, poverty, unemployment), shortages and outages (queues, power cuts, fuel crisis) or good economic news (prices fell, new jobs, pay rise).
how_it_is_calculated: Each post is checked against MARSAD word lists in Arabic (standard Arabic and common Gulf, Egyptian, Levantine and Maghrebi forms) and English. The card shows, for each list, the share of posts with at least one match and the matches per 1,000 words. The balance is the share of posts on the first side among posts with words from either side (a post with both counts on both sides). 'Not' before a word cancels it (مش مبسوط is not counted as happy). Good news share = posts with good news among posts with good news, worries or shortages.
example: In a fuel crisis, shortage posts ('طوابير', 'ما في بنزين') jump and the good news share falls from 25 % to 5 %.
good_to_know: Can be compared with official numbers (inflation, unemployment) for the same months.

title: Boycotts and buying calls
short: Calls to boycott, or to buy local
what_it_shows: How often posts call people to boycott products or companies (قاطعوا, don't buy) and how often they call to buy local or support small businesses, over time or by group.
how_it_is_calculated: Each post is checked against MARSAD word lists in Arabic (standard Arabic and common Gulf, Egyptian, Levantine and Maghrebi forms) and English. The card shows, for each list, the share of posts with at least one match and the matches per 1,000 words.
example: After a call to boycott, 'قاطعوا' posts go from 0.5 % to 8 % of posts in one week, and 'منتج محلي' posts follow.
good_to_know: Shows calls, not what people actually buy. Read the posts to see which brands or products are named.

title: Health talk
short: Asking for help, and talk about vaccines
what_it_shows: How often posts ask for help or advice (ساعدوني, any advice, therapist), mention vaccines, and take a pro-vaccine or anti-vaccine position.
how_it_is_calculated: Each post is checked against MARSAD word lists in Arabic (standard Arabic and common Gulf, Egyptian, Levantine and Maghrebi forms) and English. The card shows, for each list, the share of posts with at least one match and the matches per 1,000 words. The balance is the share of posts on the first side among posts with words from either side (a post with both counts on both sides). 'Not' before a word cancels it (مش مبسوط is not counted as happy).
example: 'ساعدوني، محتاج دكتور نفسي' counts as asking for help. Pro-vaccine share 60 % = 6 pro posts for every 4 anti posts.
good_to_know: Help seeking is shown for groups only. Most vaccine posts are neutral news: compare the pro and anti lists, not the topic list.

title: Misinformation signals
short: Conspiracy talk and miracle cures
what_it_shows: How often posts use conspiracy talk (wake up, hidden truth, الماسونية, they don't want you to know), miracle-cure claims, accusations of propaganda, and debunking words.
how_it_is_calculated: Each post is checked against MARSAD word lists in Arabic (standard Arabic and common Gulf, Egyptian, Levantine and Maghrebi forms) and English. The card shows, for each list, the share of posts with at least one match and the matches per 1,000 words.
example: 'اصحوا يا ناس، الحقيقة المخفية' is conspiracy talk; 'خلطة طبيعية تشفي من السكري' is a miracle-cure claim.
good_to_know: These are signals to read, not a fact check. Debunking posts use the same words: read the posts before reporting.

title: Issue attention
short: Which public issues get the most attention?
what_it_shows: Which of 13 public issues posts talk about: economy, health, education, security and war, environment, migration, housing, energy, rights, foreign affairs, technology, food and water, transport.
how_it_is_calculated: Each post is checked against MARSAD word lists in Arabic (standard Arabic and common Gulf, Egyptian, Levantine and Maghrebi forms) and English. The card shows, for each list, the share of posts with at least one match and the matches per 1,000 words. Split by time to see issues rise and fall.
example: Economy is named in 22 % of posts, security and war in 15 %, education in 4 %.
good_to_know: A post can be about several issues. The issue lists follow the major topics of the Comparative Agendas Project.

title: Offensive language
short: Insults and bad words, Arabic included
what_it_shows: Which posts use offensive language (insults, swear words, vulgar language), separately from hate speech.
how_it_is_calculated: A language model trained on Arabic and English offensive language data will label each post 'offensive' or 'not offensive' with a confidence score.
example: 'You idiot' is offensive but not hate speech.
good_to_know: Planned: needs MARSAD's offensive language model (or an approved public model) to be connected.

title: Hope speech
short: Posts that encourage, support and give hope
what_it_shows: Which posts express hope, encouragement or support, and how hope changes over time.
how_it_is_calculated: MARSAD's hope speech model will label each post 'hope' or 'not hope' with a confidence score.
example: 'We will rebuild, together' is hope speech.
good_to_know: Planned: needs MARSAD's hope speech model to be connected.

title: Sarcasm
short: Posts that say the opposite of what they mean
what_it_shows: Which posts are sarcastic. This also helps read the sentiment results, which often get sarcasm wrong.
how_it_is_calculated: MARSAD's sarcasm model will label each post 'sarcastic' or 'not sarcastic' with a confidence score.
example: 'Great, another power cut, just what we needed' is sarcastic.
good_to_know: Planned: needs MARSAD's sarcasm model to be connected.
